title: Adding Physician Covariates to the Wait-Time Model
text: core exposure mystery-caller study insurance type presented simulated patient. physicians identical: academic-center otolaryngologist, rural solo practitioner, urban multispecialty group physician may systematically different scheduling patterns regardless insurance. differences large unaccounted , become residual variance — noise makes harder detect insurance effect care . Adding physician-level covariates two things simultaneously: Controls confounding. Estimates insurance IRR become precise model accounts reasons wait times differ across physicians nothing insurance. Reduces residual variance. covariate explains variance outcome, unexplained (residual) variance shrinks. Smaller residual variance means narrower confidence intervals greater statistical power — may need fewer physicians follow-study. trade-degrees freedom: every covariate add costs parameters, parameters need data estimate reliably.

title: Adding Physician Covariates to the Wait-Time Model
text: Poisson regression assumes mean = variance. Real wait-time data routinely violates : physician busy weeks slow others show variance far exceeding mean (physician effect random intercept alone doesn’t absorb). overdispersion. overdispersion ratio ϕ\phi computed Pearson χ2\chi^2 / residual df. value near 1 means Poisson variance assumption holds. Values > 2 indicate problematic overdispersion.

title: Adding Physician Covariates to the Wait-Time Model
text: mysterycall_poisson_model() computes stores $overdispersion emits warning ϕ>2\phi > 2:
code: result <- mysterycall_poisson_model(   mc_data,   outcome          = "wait_days",   predictors       = c("insurance"),   random_intercept = "npi" ) result$overdispersion #> [1] 3.47 #> Warning: Overdispersion detected (phi = 3.47). Standard errors may be #>   underestimated. Consider a negative binomial model.

title: Adding Physician Covariates to the Wait-Time Model
text: Switch mysterycall_nb_model(). negative binomial distribution adds dispersion parameter θ\theta (theta) : Var(Y)=μ+μ2θ\text{Var}(Y) = \mu + \frac{\mu^2}{\theta} θ→∞\theta \\infty, variance equals mean (Poisson). θ→0\theta \0, distribution becomes overdispersed. NB model estimates θ\theta data absorbs excess variance rather fixed-effect standard errors. mysterycall_nb_model() warns : θ<1\theta < 1: extreme overdispersion even NB — consider zero-inflated model. Residual ϕ>2\phi > 2 NB fit: NB model still underfits — investigate zero-inflation outlying observations. θ>100\theta > 100: minimal overdispersion — Poisson model probably adequate; compare AIC.

title: Adding Physician Covariates to the Wait-Time Model
text: recommended multilevel negative binomial model physician covariates : log⁡(μij)=β0+β1Medicaidij+β2Incontinenceij+β3Prolapseij+β4Maleij+β5Academicij+β6Ruralij+∑k=212γkACOGDistrictkij+uj\log(\mu_{ij}) = \beta_0   + \beta_1 \text{Medicaid}_{ij}   + \beta_2 \text{Incontinence}_{ij}   + \beta_3 \text{Prolapse}_{ij}   + \beta_4 \text{Male}_{ij}   + \beta_5 \text{Academic}_{ij}   + \beta_6 \text{Rural}_{ij}   + \sum_{k=2}^{12} \gamma_k \text{ACOGDistrict}_{kij}   + u_j : Yij∼NegBin(μij,θ)Y_{ij} \sim \text{NegBin}(\mu_{ij}, \theta) ii = individual mystery call, jj = physician NPI β0\beta_0 = intercept (log expected wait reference group: BCBS + Bladder pain, female, private, urban, District ) β1\beta_1 = log IRR Medicaid vs BCBS β2,β3\beta_2, \beta_3 = log IRR scenario vs. Bladder Pain β4\beta_4 = log IRR male vs. female physician β5\beta_5 = log IRR Academic vs. Private Practice β6\beta_6 = log IRR Rural vs. Urban γk\gamma_k = fixed effect ACOG District kk (District reference) uj∼𝒩(0,σu2)u_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2) = physician-level random intercept Total fixed-effect parameters: 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 11 = 18 parameters safe n≥180n \geq 180 observations (EPV = 10).

what: Effect on power: how covariates reduce required sample size
title: Adding Physician Covariates to the Wait-Time Model
text: Adding covariates genuinely explain variance outcome reduces residual standard deviation σ\sigma. power formula detecting IRR δ\delta approximately: n≈2σ2(zα/2+zβ)2(log⁡δ)2n \approx \frac{2\sigma^2 (z_{\alpha/2} + z_\beta)^2}{(\log \delta)^2} covariate reduces σ\sigma 15%, required nn falls ≈28%\approx 28\% (1−0.8521 - 0.85^2). Approximate power analysis: detecting 25% IRR difference (80% power, α = 0.05), assuming baseline SD ≈ 30 days. Important caveats: R² figures estimates. Whether given covariate actually explains 10% 2% variance depends data. Check 1 - (residual variance covariate) / (residual variance without) fitting models. Adding covariate explains little variance increases parameters without reducing noise — effectively hurting power. EPV constraint binding: adding covariate drops EPV 10, need physicians can include .

title: Adding Physician Covariates to the Wait-Time Model
code: library(mysterycall)  # 1. Pull NPI registry data clin <- mysterycall_get_clinician_data(npi_list = mc_data$npi) mc_data <- dplyr::left_join(mc_data, clin, by = "npi")  # 2. Derive physician covariates mc_data$practice_setting <- mysterycall_classify_practice_setting(mc_data$org_name) mc_data$urbanicity       <- mysterycall_classify_ruca(mc_data$ruca_code) mc_data$acog_district    <- mysterycall_assign_region(mc_data$state, type = "acog")  # 3. Fit base Poisson to check overdispersion base_poi <- mysterycall_poisson_model(   mc_data, "wait_days",   predictors       = c("insurance", "scenario"),   random_intercept = "npi" ) base_poi$overdispersion  # if > 2, switch to NB  # 4. Fit NB with covariates nb_full <- mysterycall_nb_model(   mc_data, "wait_days",   predictors       = c("insurance", "scenario",                         "practice_setting", "urbanicity", "acog_district"),   random_intercept = "npi" ) # EPV and overdispersion warnings fire automatically if thresholds are crossed  # 5. Compare models mysterycall_select_best_model(   list(poisson_base = base_poi, nb_full = nb_full),   method = "AIC" )  # 6. Report results print(nb_full) mysterycall_irr_plot(nb_full) mysterycall_write_results_paragraph(nb_full, ref_group = "BCBS", exposure_col = "insurance")

Geocode practice addresses → lat/long geocoded <- mysterycall_geocode(   file_path           = "data/providers_with_addresses.csv",   google_maps_api_key = Sys.getenv("GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY"),   output_file_path    = "data/geocoded_providers.csv" )  # 2. title: Create Drive-Time Isochrones
text: Long batches (500+ providers) can take hour . function writes two checkpoint files output_dir every save_interval rows: isochrones_checkpoint_<timestamp>.rds — combined sf object far isochrones_checkpoint_<timestamp>.gpkg — data GeoPackage format run interrupted (network error, cluster timeout), load recent checkpoint pass completed point_index values skipped:
code: # Load the most recent checkpoint checkpoints <- list.files("data/isochrone_checkpoints", pattern = "\\.rds$",                            full.names = TRUE) partial <- readr::read_rds(sort(checkpoints, decreasing = TRUE)[1])  completed_idx <- unique(partial$point_index) message("Resuming from row ", max(completed_idx) + 1,         " (", length(completed_idx), " rows already done)")  # Pass the source file again; the function will skip completed indices isochrones_sf <- create_isochrones_for_dataframe(   input_file    = "data/iso_input.csv",   breaks        = c(30 * 60, 60 * 60, 120 * 60, 180 * 60),   api_key       = Sys.getenv("HERE_API_KEY"),   output_dir    = "data/isochrone_checkpoints",   save_interval = 100,   skip_indices  = completed_idx   # omit already-processed rows )  # Combine the checkpoint and the new results isochrones_sf <- dplyr::bind_rows(partial, isochrones_sf)

title: Data Cleaning: A Complete Workflow for Mystery Caller Studies
text: mystery caller study typically produces two raw datasets: Phase 1 — call scheduling log (physician name, practice, phone, state, NPI, insurance type) Phase 2 — call outcome log (wait time, appointment date, call result) datasets need cleaning analysis. vignette walks every mysterycall cleaning tool order typically apply , using synthetic data API keys required.

title: Data Cleaning: A Complete Workflow for Mystery Caller Studies
text: National Provider Identifier (NPI) numbers primary join key across downstream tables. Bad NPIs must caught early — row wrong NPI silently match wrong physician every subsequent lookup. mysterycall_validate_npi() applies three checks order: Strip non-digit characters leading/trailing whitespace. Require exactly 10 digits. Validate Luhn checksum (algorithm NPI standard mandates). rows npi_is_valid == TRUE survive. returned data frame strict subset input — rows ever added.
code: raw <- data.frame(   npi           = c("1234567893", "0000000000", "123456789X", NA, "1234567893 "),   physician_name = c("Smith, Alice", "Jones, Bob", "Park, Carol",                      "Lee, David", "Smith, Alice"),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  validated <- mysterycall_validate_npi(raw) #> 1 NPI value(s) are not 10 digits and were dropped before Luhn validation: 123456789 #> 1 NPI value(s) are 10 digits but failed the Luhn checksum and were dropped: 0000000000 #> Validated 4 candidate NPI(s): 1 wrong length, 1 failed Luhn, 2 passed. validated[, c("npi", "npi_is_valid", "physician_name")] #>          npi npi_is_valid physician_name #> 1 1234567893         TRUE   Smith, Alice #> 2 1234567893         TRUE   Smith, Alice

title: Data Quality: Phone Validation, Name Parsing, and Safe Joins
text: Mystery-caller studies assemble provider rosters several upstream sources (NPPES, CMS Care Compare, internal call logs) carry formatting quirks. Three categories data-quality problems arise repeatedly: Phone numbers — formatting noise ((303) 555-1234, 303.555.1234, +13035551234) area codes don’t match provider’s reported state. Physician names — single free-text name field must split first / middle / last / suffix components used call scripts de-duplication logic. Table joins — silent row multiplication right-hand table unique join key, silent data loss large fraction left-hand rows find match right. vignette walks mysterycall helpers address problem. code runs without API keys using built-package data.

title: Data Quality: Phone Validation, Name Parsing, and Safe Joins
text: North American Numbering Plan (NANP) defines structure US phone numbers: NPA (Numbering Plan Area, “area code”) must first digit 2–9, NXX (central-office code) must also first digit 2–9 must N11 service code (211, 311, …, 911). mysterycall_validate_phone() strips formatting, enforces structural rules, — optionally — checks area code belongs provider’s reported practice state using bundled inst/extdata/nanp_area_codes_us.csv lookup table.

what: The problem with silent join failures
title: Data Quality: Phone Validation, Name Parsing, and Safe Joins
text: plain dplyr::left_join() silently: Multiply rows right-hand key unique (many--one match becomes many--many). Drop rows join key types don’t match (e.g., integer vs. character NPI), causing every row land unmatched group. Return warning 40 % left-hand NPIs match right. mysterycall_safe_*_join() family wraps dplyr joins pre- post-join assertions make failures loud.

title: Data Quality: Phone Validation, Name Parsing, and Safe Joins
code: calls <- data.frame(   npi  = c("1111111111", "2222222222", "3333333333"),   date = as.Date(c("2025-01-10", "2025-01-11", "2025-01-12")),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  demographics <- data.frame(   npi    = c("1111111111", "2222222222"),   gender = c("Female", "Male"),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  # 2 of 3 left rows match → coverage = 66.7 % < 95 % threshold → error tryCatch(   suppressMessages(mysterycall_safe_left_join(     left         = calls,     right        = demographics,     by           = "npi",     label_left   = "call_log",     label_right  = "demographics",     min_coverage = 0.95   )),   error = function(e) message("Caught: ", conditionMessage(e)) ) #> Caught: Join coverage 66.7% below 95.0% threshold -- lost 1 rows. call_log -> demographics on npi.  # Lower threshold to match the actual coverage result <- suppressMessages(mysterycall_safe_left_join(   left         = calls,   right        = demographics,   by           = "npi",   label_left   = "call_log",   label_right  = "demographics",   min_coverage = 0.60 )) result #>          npi       date gender #> 1 1111111111 2025-01-10 Female #> 2 2222222222 2025-01-11   Male #> 3 3333333333 2025-01-12   <NA>

code: # Fit a Poisson mixed model: subspecialty as random intercept allows # the demo model to converge with this small simulated sample. model <- mysterycall_poisson_model(   data             = results,   outcome          = "accepted",   predictors       = "insurance_scenario",   random_intercept = "subspecialty" ) #> 24 row(s) have accepted = 0 (same-day appointments). Poisson handles zeros; verify these are intentional. #> Fitting Poisson GLMER: accepted ~ insurance_scenario + (1 | subspecialty) #> boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular') #> Convergence issues detected: #>   boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular') #> Consider simplifying predictors or using nAGQ = 1. #> Singular fit: random-intercept variance is ~0. The physician-level random effect explains little variation. #> Model fitted: n=50, physicians=6, AIC=84.2, overdispersion=0.50  # Print the incidence rate ratios (IRR) print(model) #> Poisson GLMER  n = 50  physicians = 6  AIC = 84.2  BIC = 89.9 #>   Warning: convergence warnings; singular fit #>   Reference levels: insurance_scenario='Medicaid' #>  #> Fixed effects (IRR with Wald CI): #>                        term   irr ci_lower ci_upper p_value_fmt #> 1               (Intercept) 0.259    0.124    0.544      <0.001 #> 2 insurance_scenarioPrivate 3.186    1.340    7.579       0.009 #>  #> Random intercept (subspecialty):  variance = 0.0000  SD = 0.0000  # Generate a manuscript-ready results paragraph mysterycall_write_results_paragraph(   model_result = model,   ref_group = "Private",   exposure_col = "insurance_scenario",   outcome_label = "appointment acceptance" ) #> [1] "In multivariable Poisson regression, insurance_scenario was significantly associated with appointment acceptance (see Table X). Compared with Private, callers presenting as Private had an IRR of 3.19 (95% CI 1.34-7.58; p = 0.009) for appointment acceptance."

what: 1. When to use LMM vs. Poisson/NB GLMM
title: Linear Mixed Models for Wait-Time Analysis
text: Mystery-caller studies collect wait times counts days call date offered appointment date. Two model families cover scenarios: function diagnoses distribution automatically: Skewness > 1 outcome ≥ 0: auto_log = TRUE (default) applies log1p(wait_days) fitting, back-transforms results geometric mean ratios (GMRs) reporting. Shapiro-Wilk p < 0.05 residuals: warning issued , sensitivity_poisson = "auto" (default), Poisson GLMM run alongside LMM robustness check.

title: Linear Mixed Models for Wait-Time Analysis
text: examples use synthetic dataset resembling two-wave mystery-caller study comparing Medicaid commercial insurance patients across 20 physician practices.
code: set.seed(42) n_physicians <- 20 n_calls      <- 4     # calls per physician (2 insurance types × 2 call dates)  sim_data <- data.frame(   physician  = rep(paste0("Dr", sprintf("%02d", 1:n_physicians)), each = n_calls),   insurance  = rep(c("Medicaid", "Medicaid", "BCBS", "BCBS"), n_physicians),   wave       = rep(c("Wave1", "Wave2", "Wave1", "Wave2"), n_physicians),   # Medicaid callers wait ~8 days longer on average   wait_days  = round(pmax(0,     rnorm(n_physicians * n_calls,           mean = ifelse(rep(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE), n_physicians), 29, 21),           sd   = 10)   )),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) # Add a business-days column (≈ 5/7 of calendar days) sim_data$business_days <- round(sim_data$wait_days * 0.71)  head(sim_data) #>   physician insurance  wave wait_days business_days #> 1      Dr01  Medicaid Wave1        43            31 #> 2      Dr01  Medicaid Wave2        23            16 #> 3      Dr01      BCBS Wave1        25            18 #> 4      Dr01      BCBS Wave2        27            19 #> 5      Dr02  Medicaid Wave1        33            23 #> 6      Dr02  Medicaid Wave2        28            20

title: Linear Mixed Models for Wait-Time Analysis
text: satisfy M&M promise supplemental table comparing calendar-day business-day wait times, use mysterycall_calendar_sensitivity(): comparison table: Whether term directions consistent across measurement approaches: ready--paste supplemental paragraph:
code: sens <- mysterycall_calendar_sensitivity(   data             = sim_data,   calendar_col     = "wait_days",   business_col     = "business_days",   predictors       = c("insurance", "wave"),   random_intercept = "physician",   ref_label        = "BCBS (commercial)",   supp_table_num   = "S2" ) #> Fitting calendar-days model (wait_days)... #> Fitting business-days model (business_days)... sens$summary_table #>                Term                Calendar days                 Business days #> 1 insuranceMedicaid 7.9 (3.4 to 12.5), p = 0.001   5.7 (2.4 to 8.9), p = 0.001 #> 2         waveWave2  -0.5 (-5.1 to 4), p = 0.822 -0.5 (-3.7 to 2.8), p = 0.775 #>   Consistent #> 1        Yes #> 2        Yes sens$all_consistent #> [1] TRUE cat(sens$paragraph) #> As a pre-specified sensitivity analysis, we repeated the secondary wait-time analysis substituting business days (Monday through Friday, excluding the 11 U.S. federal holidays) for calendar days. Business days were computed using the R package \emph{bizdays} with a US Federal holiday calendar. The calendar-day model included 80 observations with a recorded appointment date; the business-day model included 80 observations. Both models used the same mixed-effects linear regression specification (insurance and wave as fixed effect compared with BCBS (commercial) (reference); physician practice as random intercept). Results were directionally consistent across both metrics for all comparisons. Business-day estimates were on average 81% of calendar-day estimates (median ratio = 0.81), consistent with the expected 5/7 weekday fraction. Shapiro-Wilk normality tests on model residuals: calendar-day model: W = 0.985, p = 0.499; business-day model: W = 0.987, p = 0.595. Full results are presented in Supplemental Table S2.

title: Mystery Caller Workflow: From Raw Data to Manuscript
text: Mystery-caller (secret-shopper) studies measure disparities healthcare access trained callers pose patients requesting appointments different insurance types. physician sampling frame called per insurance type; caller records whether appointment offered , , many business days earliest available slot. mysterycall package provides structured pipeline raw call logs manuscript-ready statistics, covering quality control, deduplication, descriptive summaries, regression modeling, sensitivity analyses.

title: Mystery Caller Workflow: From Raw Data to Manuscript
text: construct 200-row data frame representing 100 physician offices, called twice — Medicaid Blue Cross/Blue Shield.
code: suppressMessages({   library(mysterycall)    set.seed(42)   n_phy  <- 100L   ids    <- sprintf("%03d", seq_len(n_phy))   phones <- paste0("555-", sprintf("%04d", seq_len(n_phy)))    raw_df <- data.frame(     id_number             = rep(ids, each = 2L),     phone                 = rep(phones, each = 2L),     physician_information = paste0("Dr. Physician ", rep(ids, each = 2L)),     insurance             = rep(c("Medicaid", "Blue Cross/Blue Shield"), n_phy),     stringsAsFactors      = FALSE   )    raw_df$reason_for_exclusions <- sample(     c("Able to contact", "Physician not available", "Number disconnected"),     200L, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.70, 0.20, 0.10)   )    # Appointment wait times only for successfully-contacted rows   raw_df$business_days_until_appointment <- ifelse(     raw_df$reason_for_exclusions == "Able to contact",     rpois(200L, lambda = 14L) + 1L,     NA_integer_   )    # Medicaid acceptance column: realistic for Medicaid rows, boilerplate for BCBS   medicaid_vals <- sample(     c(       "Yes they accept Medicaid",       "No",       "No answer, unable to determine if they accept Medicaid."     ),     200L, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.55, 0.30, 0.15)   )   raw_df$does_the_physician_accept_medicaid <- ifelse(     raw_df$insurance == "Medicaid",     medicaid_vals,     "NA as this was a Blue Cross/Blue Shield call."   )    raw_df$scenario <- sample(     c("HIP scenario", "SHOULDER scenario", "KNEE scenario"),     200L, replace = TRUE   )   raw_df$gender <- sample(c("Male", "Female"), 200L, replace = TRUE)   raw_df$state  <- sample(     c(       "Colorado", "Texas", "California", "New York", "Florida",       "Illinois", "Pennsylvania", "Ohio", "Georgia", "Michigan"     ),     200L, replace = TRUE   )   raw_df$notes <- NA_character_ })  dim(raw_df) #> [1] 200  11 head(raw_df[, c("id_number", "phone", "insurance",                 "reason_for_exclusions", "business_days_until_appointment")]) #>   id_number    phone              insurance   reason_for_exclusions #> 1       001 555-0001               Medicaid     Number disconnected #> 2       001 555-0001 Blue Cross/Blue Shield     Number disconnected #> 3       002 555-0002               Medicaid         Able to contact #> 4       002 555-0002 Blue Cross/Blue Shield Physician not available #> 5       003 555-0003               Medicaid         Able to contact #> 6       003 555-0003 Blue Cross/Blue Shield         Able to contact #>   business_days_until_appointment #> 1                              NA #> 2                              NA #> 3                              11 #> 4                              NA #> 5                              12 #> 6                              13

title: Power Analysis and Sample Size for Mystery Caller Studies
text: sampling frame known, finite directory NN providers, Cochran (1977) formula gives minimum sample nn estimated proportion (e.g. acceptance rate) within ee percentage points 95 % confidence: n0=Zα/22⋅p(1−p)e2→n=n01+n0−1N n_0 = \frac{Z^2_{\alpha/2} \cdot p(1-p)}{e^2} \qquad\longrightarrow\qquad n = \frac{n_0}{1 + \frac{n_0 - 1}{N}} Setting p=0.5p = 0.5 (maximum variance) Z0.025=1.96Z_{0.025} = 1.96 simplifies : n=N1+Ne2 n = \frac{N}{1 + N e^2} finite-population correction factor (1+n0−1N)−1\left(1 + \frac{n_0-1}{N}\right)^{-1} makes n<n0n < n_0 whenever sample represents meaningful fraction directory.

title: Power Analysis and Sample Size for Mystery Caller Studies
text: Required sample sizes across directory sizes precision targets. Key insight: moderate--large directories (N ≥ 400), ±5% target requires roughly 200 providers regardless large directory grows — finite-population correction becomes negligible.
code: # 800 OB-GYNs in target region — need acceptance rate within ±5 percentage points res_800 <- mysterycall_cochran_n(N = 800, margin_of_error = 0.05) cat(sprintf(   "N = %d providers, target ME ±%.0f%%: sample n = %d (achieved ME = ±%.1f%%)\n",   res_800$N, res_800$margin_of_error * 100,   res_800$n, res_800$effective_margin * 100 )) #> N = 800 providers, target ME ±5%: sample n = 267 (achieved ME = ±5.0%) # Show how n changes across directory sizes and margin-of-error targets grid <- expand.grid(   N  = c(100, 200, 400, 800, 1600),   me = c(0.03, 0.05, 0.10) )  grid$n <- mapply(   function(N, me) mysterycall_cochran_n(N, me)$n,   grid$N, grid$me )  pivot_tbl <- stats::reshape(   grid,   idvar = "N", timevar = "me", direction = "wide" ) names(pivot_tbl) <- c("Directory size (N)", "n at ±3%", "n at ±5%", "n at ±10%")  knitr::kable(   pivot_tbl,   caption = "Required sample sizes across directory sizes and precision targets." )

Required sample size per arm IRR = 1.40 across different reference wait-time assumptions. Interpretation: wait times get shorter (fewer days), Poisson rate becomes smaller variable relative mean, providers needed detect proportional difference.
code: lambda_vals <- c(5, 7, 10, 14, 21, 30)  n_by_lambda <- vapply(lambda_vals, function(lam)   mysterycall_poisson_power(irr = 1.40, lambda_ref = lam, power = 0.80,                              both_arms = TRUE)$n_per_arm,   numeric(1)) #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=5.0, lambda_trt=7.0 | n_per_arm=24, n_total=24, calls=48 #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=7.0, lambda_trt=9.8 | n_per_arm=17, n_total=17, calls=34 #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=10.0, lambda_trt=14.0 | n_per_arm=12, n_total=12, calls=24 #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=14.0, lambda_trt=19.6 | n_per_arm=9, n_total=9, calls=18 #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=21.0, lambda_trt=29.4 | n_per_arm=6, n_total=6, calls=12 #> Poisson power: IRR=1.40, lambda_ref=30.0, lambda_trt=42.0 | n_per_arm=4, n_total=4, calls=8  lam_df <- data.frame(lambda_ref = lambda_vals, n_per_arm = n_by_lambda)  ggplot(lam_df, aes(x = lambda_ref, y = n_per_arm)) +   geom_col(fill = "#2166AC", alpha = 0.8) +   geom_text(aes(label = n_per_arm), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.5) +   labs(     title   = "Sample size sensitivity to reference wait time",     subtitle = "IRR = 1.40, 80% power, paired design",     x       = "Reference-arm mean wait time (days)",     y       = "Required providers per arm"   ) +   theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

what: Where to get the crosswalk file

text: USDA ERS publishes ZIP--RUCA crosswalk : https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/rural-urban-commuting-area-codes Download ZIP code file (census tract file). 2023, file named something like ruca2010revised.xlsx. what: Step 1: Load and clean the crosswalk
title: Provider Classification and Demographic Enrichment
text: Critical: Always read ZIP codes character, integer. ZIP codes like 01234 (Massachusetts) lose leading zero read numeric, causing New England providers fail join.
code: library(readr)  ruca_crosswalk <- read_csv(   "data-raw/ruca2010revised.csv",   col_types = cols(     ZIP_CODE = col_character(),  # keep leading zeros: "01234" not 1234     RUCA1    = col_double()   ) ) |>   dplyr::select(zip5 = ZIP_CODE, ruca_code = RUCA1) |>   dplyr::distinct(zip5, .keep_all = TRUE)  # one row per ZIP

what: Step 2: Prepare the ZIP column in your roster
title: Provider Classification and Demographic Enrichment
text: NPPES exports ZIP codes column named addresses_postal_code. column often contains 9-digit ZIP+4 codes (e.g., 80204-2127). need 5-digit base ZIP .
code: roster <- roster |>   dplyr::mutate(     zip5 = stringr::str_sub(addresses_postal_code, 1L, 5L)   )

what: Step 3: Join the crosswalk using mysterycall_safe_left_join()
title: Provider Classification and Demographic Enrichment
text: mysterycall_safe_left_join() performs several safety checks automatically: asserts ruca_crosswalk unique keys zip5 (duplicate ZIP rows fan roster). coerces mismatched column types (e.g., one side zip5 integer character) prevent silent zero-match joins. reports join coverage: fraction roster rows found matching ZIP crosswalk. stops informative error coverage falls min_coverage. coverage 90%, inspect unmatched ZIPs: Post office box ZIP codes, US territories (Guam, Puerto Rico, US Virgin Islands), military APO/FPO addresses common sources unmatched ZIPs. text: National Provider Identifier (NPI) registry publish physician birth year. deliberate privacy protection. However, registry publish medical school graduation year, strong proxy age. mysterycall_impute_age() converts graduation year estimated current age using formula: age_offset (default 27) median age US medical school graduation. method validated Doximity birth-year data 32,000 OB/GYN physicians (r = 0.962, mean absolute error = 2.1 years) 348 ENT physicians (r = 0.957, MAE = 1.7 years).

code: roster <- roster |>   dplyr::mutate(     age_imputed = mysterycall_impute_age(       graduation_year,       ref_year   = 2023L,  # pin to your data collection year       age_offset = 27L     # validated median age at US med school graduation     )   )

Investigate proceeding. Implausible ages (min_age = 25 max_age = 90): Values outside range set NA warning. physician graduated 1924 computed age 129 2023 — almost certainly data entry error NPPES. Check rows manually.

title: Statistical Analysis of Mystery-Caller Data
text: mystery-caller study (also called audit study correspondence study) controlled experiment used detect discrimination health-care access. central idea elegantly simple: trained research callers—posing prospective patients—telephone physician offices attempt schedule new-patient appointment. callers follow standardized script, vary characteristic investigation (commonly insurance type), record outcome call, design provides direct, high-fidelity measure real-world access disparities surveys claims data replicate. method pioneered health disparities research Asplin colleagues (2005) since applied dozens specialty access questions: Medicaid patients wait longer orthopedic consultation? uninsured callers offered fewer -month appointments commercially insured callers? mysterycall package implements statistical routines needed answer questions correctly.

title: Statistical Analysis of Mystery-Caller Data
text: Every mystery-caller call produces exactly two outcomes capture different dimensions access: Appointment offered (binary, 0/1). office offer caller new-patient appointment ? value 0 means office declined, said accepting new patients, gave number disconnected never answered. value 1 means appointment scheduled offered. primary disparity outcome. Wait time business days (count ≥ 0). Among calls resulted offered appointment (appointment_offered == 1), many business days elapsed date call earliest available appointment? non-negative integer count analyzed Poisson generalized linear model. important understand two outcomes measure different barriers. Medicaid patient might face binary access barrier (turned away entirely) wait-time barrier (accepted, wait longer). reported; reporting one paints incomplete picture.

what: Within-Physician Correlation: Why Multilevel Models Are Essential
title: Statistical Analysis of Mystery-Caller Data
text: critical design feature separates mystery-caller data simple cross-sectional surveys physician (identified National Provider Identifier, NPI) called multiple times different insurance types. typical study design calls physician Medicaid patient, privately insured patient, Medicare patient, uninsured patient—producing four observations per physician. means observations independent. Two calls physician share physician’s baseline acceptance behavior, scheduling culture, practice-level factors (urban vs. rural, solo vs. group practice, etc.). fit ordinary logistic Poisson regression treats every call independent observation, : Underestimate standard errors (effectively overcounting information data). Report confidence intervals narrow p-values small—inflating Type error rate. Fail separate within-physician insurance effect (physician behave differently depending calling?) -physician effect (high-Medicaid-accepting physicians differ systematically low-accepting physicians?). solution add physician-level random intercept model. random intercept absorbs physician’s baseline tendency offer appointments (baseline wait-time level), leaving fixed effects estimate pure insurance-type contrast within physicians. standard generalized linear mixed-effects model (GLMM) approach, implemented R lme4 package.

title: Statistical Analysis of Mystery-Caller Data
text: Wait time business days count variable: takes non-negative integer values (0, 1, 2, 3, …), negative (physician offer appointment past), distribution typically right-skewed concentration small values long upper tail. properties disqualify ordinary least-squares linear regression primary analysis: Linear regression assumes continuous, symmetric, normally distributed outcome. Wait-time data violate three assumptions. Linear regression can predict negative wait times, nonsensical. equal-variance (homoscedasticity) assumption fails: variance wait times tends grow mean (Poisson processes variance = mean definition). Poisson regression models natural logarithm expected count linear function covariates: log⁡(E[Y])=𝐗𝛃\log\!\bigl(E[Y]\bigr) = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} exponentiated coefficients exp⁡(βk)\exp(\beta_k) incidence rate ratios (IRRs), natural clinical interpretation: IRR 1.40 Medicaid vs. Private insurance means Medicaid patients waited 40 % longer privately insured patients, average, adjusting covariates model. Right-skewed wait-time distribution Medicaid callers (simulated). mysterycall_plot_distribution() returns raw sqrt-scaled panels — sqrt panel makes long upper tail visible without distorting modal value.

Near-zero -physician variance (physicians truly behave identically—mean random intercept unnecessary). Choosing nAGQ: mystery-caller datasets (≥ 30 physicians, balanced design), default nAGQ = 1 (Laplace approximation) provides excellent accuracy. small datasets (< 30 physicians highly unbalanced designs), setting nAGQ = 3 nAGQ = 5 uses adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature, computationally expensive accurate. difference estimates typically negligible large samples.

text: ci_method argument supports three approaches: "wilson" (default): Wilson score interval preferred choice proportions. Unlike Wald interval (p̂±1.96SE\hat{p} \pm 1.96\,\text{SE}), Wilson interval always within [0,1][0, 1] excellent coverage probability even nn small true proportion near 0 1: p̃±zα/21+zα/22/np̂(1−p̂)n+zα/224n2,p̃=p̂+zα/22/(2n)1+zα/22/n\tilde{p} \pm \frac{z_{\alpha/2}}{1 + z_{\alpha/2}^2/n}   \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n} + \frac{z_{\alpha/2}^2}{4n^2}}, \qquad   \tilde{p} = \frac{\hat{p} + z_{\alpha/2}^2/(2n)}{1 + z_{\alpha/2}^2/n} Use situations. - "exact" (Clopper-Pearson): exact binomial interval. guaranteed coverage ≥ 95 % cost conservative (wide). Use want conservative bound exact coverage guarantee matters (e.g., regulatory submissions). - "wald": standard normal approximation. Appropriate n ≥ 50 per group proportion 0.15 0.85. Included compatibility older literature rarely recommended. Appointment-offered rates insurance type 95 % Wilson score confidence intervals. Private insurance reference group (dashed line). Medicaid Uninsured callers face largest absolute deficits. mysterycall_plot_disparities() supports three metrics — switch metric: Absolute difference acceptance rate (percentage points) versus Private insurance. Negative values indicate lower appointment-offered rates. Relative risk offered appointment versus Private insurance. Values 1 indicate lower rates group.
code: # Build a representative disparities table from synthetic data set.seed(99) n_per   <- 200L ins     <- rep(c("Medicaid", "Medicare", "Private", "Uninsured"), each = n_per) probs   <- rep(c(0.64, 0.84, 0.91, 0.54), each = n_per) demo_df <- data.frame(insurance = ins,                        accepted  = rbinom(length(ins), 1L, probs))  disp_tbl <- mysterycall_disparities_table(demo_df, "accepted", "insurance",                                            ref_group = "Private")  # One call replaces 30+ lines of manual ggplot2 mysterycall_plot_disparities(disp_tbl, metric = "rate") #> `height` was translated to `width`. mysterycall_plot_disparities(disp_tbl, metric = "abs_diff",                               title = "Absolute disparity (pp vs. Private)") #> `height` was translated to `width`. mysterycall_plot_disparities(disp_tbl, metric = "rel_risk",                               title = "Relative risk vs. Private") #> `height` was translated to `width`. #> Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range #> (`geom_text()`).

title: Statistical Analysis of Mystery-Caller Data
text: Two corrections implemented mysterycall_multiple_comparison_adjust(): Bonferroni correction: Divide α\alpha threshold number tests mm (equivalently, multiply p-value mm, capping 1.0). adjusted p-value test kk : pkBonf=min⁡(m⋅pk,1)p_k^{\text{Bonf}} = \min(m \cdot p_k,\; 1) controls family-wise error rate exactly underpowered mm large. Holm-Bonferroni (Holm’s step-) correction: Sort raw p-values smallest largest: p(1)≤p(2)≤⋯≤p(m)p_{(1)} \le p_{(2)} \le \cdots \le p_{(m)}. adjusted p-value kk-th ordered test : p(k)Holm=min⁡(maxj≤k[(m−j+1)p(j)],1)p_{(k)}^{\text{Holm}} = \min\!\Bigl(\max_{j \le k}\!\bigl[(m - j + 1)\,p_{(j)}\bigr],\; 1\Bigr) Holm-Bonferroni uniformly powerful Bonferroni still controlling family-wise error rate. Prefer Holm-Bonferroni almost situations. Key insight output: Medicare comparison (raw p = 0.017) crosses Bonferroni-corrected threshold 0.017 (= 0.05/3) declared non-significant Bonferroni. However, remains significant Holm correction. illustrates Bonferroni can overly conservative: ignores ordering evidence across tests.
code: # Extract the raw p-values from the disparities table raw_p <- disparities$p_value names(raw_p) <- disparities$insurance[disparities$insurance != "Private"] raw_p #>    Medicaid    Medicare   Uninsured #>   < 0.0001      0.0170    < 0.0001  # Apply Bonferroni and Holm-Bonferroni corrections adj_results <- mysterycall_multiple_comparison_adjust(   p_values   = raw_p,   method     = c("bonferroni", "holm"),  # compute both   alpha      = 0.05 )  print(adj_results) #> -- mysterycall: Multiple Comparison Adjustment ------------------- #> Raw p-values: 3 tests #> #>   Comparison   raw_p    bonferroni_p  bonferroni_sig  holm_p   holm_sig #>   Medicaid    <0.001      <0.001          ***          <0.001     *** #>   Medicare     0.017       0.051           .            0.034      * #>   Uninsured   <0.001      <0.001          ***          <0.001     *** #> #> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 #> #> Note: Holm correction is uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni. #>       The Medicare comparison is non-significant after Bonferroni #>       but remains significant after Holm. Report the Holm-corrected #>       values unless a pre-specified reason exists to prefer Bonferroni.

BCa interval endpoints : θ̂α1*,θ̂α2*\hat{\theta}^*_{\alpha_1}, \quad \hat{\theta}^*_{\alpha_2} α1=Φ(ẑ0+ẑ0+zα/21−̂(ẑ0+zα/2))\alpha_1 = \Phi\!\left(\hat{z}_0 + \dfrac{\hat{z}_0 + z_{\alpha/2}}{1 - \hat{}(\hat{z}_0 + z_{\alpha/2})}\right) α2=Φ(ẑ0+ẑ0+z1−α/21−̂(ẑ0+z1−α/2))\alpha_2 = \Phi\!\left(\hat{z}_0 + \dfrac{\hat{z}_0 + z_{1-\alpha/2}}{1 - \hat{}(\hat{z}_0 + z_{1-\alpha/2})}\right), ẑ0\hat{z}_0 bias-correction constant ̂\hat{} acceleration constant estimated jackknife leave-one-statistics. Simulated bootstrap distribution Medicaid minus Private appointment-rate difference (B = 2 000 replicates, physician-level resampling). observed difference shown solid vertical line; BCa 95 % CI endpoints dashed.
code: set.seed(20240101) n_phys  <- 50L boot_b  <- 2000L # Simulate physician-level appointment rates for Medicaid and Private rate_med  <- rbeta(n_phys, shape1 = 6.4, shape2 = 3.6) rate_priv <- rbeta(n_phys, shape1 = 9.1, shape2 = 0.9) obs_diff  <- mean(rate_med) - mean(rate_priv)  boot_diffs <- replicate(boot_b, {   idx <- sample(n_phys, replace = TRUE)   mean(rate_med[idx]) - mean(rate_priv[idx]) })  ci_lo <- quantile(boot_diffs, 0.025) ci_hi <- quantile(boot_diffs, 0.975)  boot_plot_df <- data.frame(diff = boot_diffs)  ggplot2::ggplot(boot_plot_df, ggplot2::aes(x = diff)) +   ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#4393c3", color = "white",                            linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.85) +   ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = obs_diff, linewidth = 1, color = "#c0392b") +   ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = c(ci_lo, ci_hi),                        linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed", color = "#333333") +   ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +   ggplot2::labs(     x = "Medicaid - Private appointment-rate difference",     y = "Bootstrap replicates"   ) +   ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

text: Important: cluster = "npi" argument resamples whole physicians (rather individual calls) bootstrap replicate. respects within-physician clustering structure. resample individual calls independently, break dependence structure CIs anti-conservative (narrow).

text: Translating statistical output clear, accurate prose one time-consuming parts manuscript writing. function mysterycall_write_results_paragraph() accepts key model objects returns formatted results paragraph following APA 7th edition style conventions reporting guidelines JAMA NEJM observational health disparities research. APA-style formatting conventions used: - p-values expressed exact values (“p < 0.05” except p < 0.001) - 95 % CIs reported every effect estimate - Sample sizes stated upfront - Adjustment method named explicitly (“Holm-Bonferroni correction”) - Effect direction stated plain language (“waited 42% longer”) technical notation (IRR 1.42)
code: results_text <- mysterycall_write_results_paragraph(   poisson_model      = poisson_fit,   disparities_table  = adj_full,           # version with adjusted p-values   bootstrap_ci       = boot_result,   outcome_label      = "new-patient appointment",   insurance_ref      = "Private",   alpha              = 0.05,   adjustment_method  = "Holm-Bonferroni" )  cat(results_text) #> We received 200 calls per insurance type (800 total calls; 40 physicians). #> The overall appointment-offered rate was 91.0% (95% Wilson CI: 86.0%-94.5%) #> for privately insured callers, compared with 64.0% (95% CI: 57.2%-70.3%) #> for Medicaid callers, 84.0% (95% CI: 78.1%-88.8%) for Medicare callers, #> and 54.0% (95% CI: 47.1%-60.8%) for uninsured callers. Medicaid callers #> were offered appointments at a rate 27.0 percentage points lower than #> privately insured callers (relative risk 0.70; 95% BCa bootstrap CI: #> -34.9 to -19.1 pp; Holm-adjusted p < .001). Uninsured callers had the #> lowest appointment-offered rate, 37.0 percentage points below the privately #> insured rate (relative risk 0.59; Holm-adjusted p < .001). Medicare callers #> had a 7.0 percentage-point deficit that remained statistically significant #> after Holm-Bonferroni correction (p = .034). #> #> Among callers offered appointments, we modelled wait time in business days #> using a Poisson generalized linear mixed-effects model with a physician-level #> random intercept to account for within-physician correlation (40 physicians; #> intraclass correlation coefficient 0.089). The Pearson chi-squared #> overdispersion ratio was 1.08, indicating adequate model fit. Medicaid #> callers waited 42% longer than privately insured callers (incidence rate #> ratio [IRR] 1.42; 95% profile-likelihood CI: 1.18-1.70; p < .001). #> Uninsured callers waited 29% longer (IRR 1.29; 95% CI: 1.06-1.57; p = .012). #> No statistically significant wait-time difference was observed for Medicare #> callers (IRR 1.08; 95% CI: 0.89-1.31; p = .441).

code: set.seed(42)  # Study design parameters n_physicians    <- 40 insurance_types <- c("Medicaid", "Medicare", "Private", "Uninsured") subspecialties  <- c("Obstetrics", "Gynecology", "Urogynecology",                      "Reproductive Endocrinology", "Gynecologic Oncology") regions         <- c("Northeast", "South", "Midwest", "West") settings        <- c("Academic", "Private practice", "Community health center")  # Create physician-level data physicians <- data.frame(   npi             = sprintf("%010d", seq_len(n_physicians)),   physician_gender = sample(c("Female", "Male"), n_physicians,                             replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.75, 0.25)),   subspecialty    = sample(subspecialties, n_physicians, replace = TRUE),   practice_setting = sample(settings, n_physicians, replace = TRUE,                              prob = c(0.30, 0.50, 0.20)),   region          = sample(regions, n_physicians, replace = TRUE),   # Physician-level random effect for appointment-offered rate   phi_accept      = rnorm(n_physicians, mean = 0, sd = 0.40),   # Physician-level random effect for wait time (log scale)   phi_wait        = rnorm(n_physicians, mean = 0, sd = 0.30),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  # Create call-level data: each physician called once per insurance type calls_list <- lapply(seq_len(n_physicians), function(i) {   ph <- physicians[i, ]    # Insurance-type fixed effects on appointment-offered rate (log-odds scale)   # Reference = Private; Medicaid is hardest to get, Uninsured also hard   insurance_logodds <- c(     Medicaid  = -1.20,     Medicare  = -0.30,     Private   =  0.00,     Uninsured = -1.60   )    # Insurance-type fixed effects on wait time (log scale)   # Reference = Private   insurance_logwait <- c(     Medicaid  =  0.35,     Medicare  =  0.08,     Private   =  0.00,     Uninsured =  0.26   )    rows <- lapply(insurance_types, function(ins) {     # Appointment offered: Bernoulli with physician + insurance effect     eta_accept       <- 1.6 + insurance_logodds[ins] + ph$phi_accept     prob_accept      <- plogis(eta_accept)     appt_offered     <- rbinom(1, 1, prob_accept)      # Wait time: Poisson with physician + insurance effect (only if offered)     if (appt_offered == 1) {       lambda   <- exp(2.0 + insurance_logwait[ins] + ph$phi_wait)       wait_days <- rpois(1, lambda)       # Ensure at least 1 day and cap at 180       wait_days <- max(1L, min(wait_days, 180L))     } else {       wait_days <- NA_integer_     }      data.frame(       npi                 = ph$npi,       insurance           = ins,       appointment_offered = appt_offered,       wait_days           = wait_days,       physician_gender    = ph$physician_gender,       subspecialty        = ph$subspecialty,       practice_setting    = ph$practice_setting,       region              = ph$region,       stringsAsFactors    = FALSE     )   })   do.call(rbind, rows) })  mc_data <- do.call(rbind, calls_list) mc_data$insurance <- factor(mc_data$insurance,                              levels = c("Private", "Medicaid", "Medicare",                                         "Uninsured"))  # Verify dimensions dim(mc_data) #> [1] 160   8  # Show first six rows head(mc_data) #>          npi insurance appointment_offered wait_days physician_gender #>  0000000001  Private                   1        6         Female #>  0000000001  Medicaid                  0        NA        Female #>  0000000001  Medicare                  1        9         Female #>  0000000001  Uninsured                 0        NA        Female #>  0000000002  Private                   1        4           Male #>  0000000002  Medicaid                  1       14           Male #>    subspecialty practice_setting    region #>     Obstetrics  Private practice  Northeast #>     Obstetrics  Private practice  Northeast #>     Obstetrics  Private practice  Northeast #>     Obstetrics  Private practice  Northeast #>     Gynecology  Academic          South #>     Gynecology  Academic          South

title: Generating Publication Tables
text: Parameter details: covariates — character vector column names appear row groups table. function detects whether variable continuous (numeric integer > 5 unique values) categorical (factor character, numeric ≤ 5 unique values) formats accordingly. stratify_by — column whose unique values become stratification columns. Pass NULL generate unstratified table single “Overall” column. include_overall — TRUE, column labelled “Overall” prepended stratification columns, showing counts percentages across full sample regardless stratum. cont_stats — controls continuous variables (e.g., wait_days) summarized: * "mean_sd": Mean ± SD, appropriate distribution approximately normal. * "median_iqr": Median [IQR], appropriate right-skewed variables like wait times. * c("mean_sd", "median_iqr"): rows printed. Useful supplements data-quality tables rarely appropriate primary manuscript table. p_value — TRUE, column p-values appended. categorical variables, function runs Pearson chi-squared test; expected cell count min_cell, switches Fisher’s exact test. continuous variables, runs Kruskal-Wallis test (regardless whether cont_stats "mean_sd" "median_iqr") mystery-caller data rarely satisfy normality assumptions required standard t-test ANOVA. Interpreting p-values context: mystery-caller study, p-values Table 1 test whether sampling balanced insurance type. test primary hypothesis (appointment disparity). significant p-value Table 1 means providers assigned Medicaid private-insurance call scenarios differ characteristic, relevant split done something mysterycall_split_and_save(). split random (), Table 1 p-values non-significant. variable_labels — named character vector names column names data values display labels appear table. translate snake_case column names mixed-case, abbreviation-spelled-labels journals require. min_cell — default 5, following standard Fisher’s exact test threshold used biostatistics textbooks. subspecialty comparisons rare specialties (e.g., Reproductive Endocrinology appears < 5% rows), threshold trigger Fisher’s exact test automatically. Note function prints message switches tests:
code: tbl1 <- mysterycall_table1(   data             = analysis_data,   covariates       = c("age_category", "gender_std", "subspecialty",                        "practice_setting", "region_std", "ruca_category"),   stratify_by      = "insurance_type",   include_overall  = TRUE,   cont_stats       = "median_iqr",    # "mean_sd", "median_iqr", or c("mean_sd","median_iqr")   digits           = 1,               # decimal places for percentages   p_value          = TRUE,            # adds chi-sq / Kruskal-Wallis p-value column   min_cell         = 5,               # use Fisher's exact test when expected cell < 5   variable_labels  = c(     age_category     = "Provider age, years",     gender_std       = "Physician sex",     subspecialty     = "Subspecialty",     practice_setting = "Practice setting",     region_std       = "US Census region",     ruca_category    = "Rurality (RUCA category)"   ) )  print(tbl1) # Note: Using Fisher's exact test for 'subspecialty' (minimum expected # cell count = 2.3, below threshold of 5).

text: journals — conference poster sessions — expect significance stars (* p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; *** p < 0.001) alongside adjusted p-values. code: # Extract numeric p-values (assumes a 'p_numeric' column in the result) disp_tbl$stars <- dplyr::case_when(   disp_tbl$p_numeric < 0.001 ~ "***",   disp_tbl$p_numeric < 0.01  ~ "**",   disp_tbl$p_numeric < 0.05  ~ "*",   TRUE                        ~ "" )  # Combine with formatted p-value for display disp_tbl$p_display <- paste0(   formatC(disp_tbl$p_numeric, format = "f", digits = 3),   disp_tbl$stars )

This disparity persisted after adjustment for physician sex, subspecialty, practice setting, US Census region, and rurality (aOR 0.63, 95% CI [0.53, 0.75]; p < 0.001). Among subspecialties, the largest disparity was observed in Urogynecology (aOR 0.44, 95% CI [0.28, 0.70]; p < 0.001) and the smallest in Gynecologic Oncology (aOR 0.81, 95% CI [0.58, 1.13]; p = 0.21).

text: Mystery-caller wait times measured business days — weekends US federal holidays excluded. mysterycall_count_business_days() counts business days two dates; mysterycall_business_days() applies calculation every row data frame. Business-day wait times computed mysterycall_business_days().
code: # How many business days between a call on a Monday and an appointment on # Friday of the following week?  (Calendar days = 11; business days = 10) bd <- mysterycall_count_business_days(   start_date = "2024-03-04",   # Monday   end_date   = "2024-03-15"    # Friday two weeks later ) cat("Business days:", bd, "\n") #> Business days: 9 # Apply to a data frame of completed calls calls_df <- data.frame(   npi       = paste0("NPI-", 1:6),   insurance = c("Medicaid", "Private", "Medicaid", "Private", "Medicare", "Uninsured"),   call_date = as.Date(c("2024-03-04", "2024-03-04", "2024-03-11",                          "2024-03-11", "2024-03-18", "2024-03-18")),   appt_date = as.Date(c("2024-03-25", "2024-03-12", "2024-04-01",                          "2024-03-19", "2024-03-27", "2024-04-08")) )  # mysterycall_business_days() column params: call_col, appt_col, result_col calls_with_bd <- mysterycall_business_days(   data       = calls_df,   call_col   = "call_date",   appt_col   = "appt_date",   result_col = "wait_days" ) #> Business days computed for 6/6 row(s); stored in column 'wait_days'.  knitr::kable(   calls_with_bd[, c("npi", "insurance", "call_date", "appt_date", "wait_days")],   col.names = c("NPI", "Insurance", "Call date", "Appt date", "Wait (business days)"),   caption   = "Business-day wait times computed by `mysterycall_business_days()`." )

title: End-to-End Mystery-Caller Workflow Orchestration
text: mysterycall_caller_reliability() computes Cohen’s kappa (categorical outcomes) intraclass correlation coefficient (numeric outcomes) records audited two callers.
code: set.seed(7) # Long-format audit sample: each record appears twice — once per caller n_records <- 30L audit_long <- data.frame(   record_id  = rep(1:n_records, 2),   caller     = rep(c("Alice", "Bob"), each = n_records),   appt_offered = c(     sample(c("Yes", "No"), n_records, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.72, 0.28)),     sample(c("Yes", "No"), n_records, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.68, 0.32))   ) )  rel <- mysterycall_caller_reliability(   data        = audit_long,   caller_col  = "caller",   outcome_col = "appt_offered",   type        = "kappa" )  print(rel) #> -- mysterycall_caller_reliability -- #> Method       : kappa  #> Statistic    : 0.3478  #> 95% CI       : [ -0.0087 , 0.7043 ] #> N pairs      : 30  #> Interpretation: fair (Landis & Koch)

title: End-to-End Mystery-Caller Workflow Orchestration
text: mysterycall_call_productivity() tallies completed, pending, failed calls caller returns summary data frame QC review. Table: Per-caller productivity mysterycall_call_productivity().
code: set.seed(8) n_rows <- 80L prod_df <- data.frame(   caller           = sample(c("Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dana"),                              n_rows, replace = TRUE),   call_date        = sample(seq(as.Date("2024-02-01"), as.Date("2024-03-31"),                                  by = "day"), n_rows, replace = TRUE),   appointment_offered = sample(c(1L, 1L, 1L, 0L), n_rows, replace = TRUE) )  prod <- mysterycall_call_productivity(   data        = prod_df,   caller_col  = "caller",   date_col    = "call_date",   outcome_col = "appointment_offered" )  knitr::kable(   prod$summary,   caption = "Per-caller productivity from `mysterycall_call_productivity()`." )

title: Mystery Caller Study Tools for Healthcare Access Research
text: Measuring patient access healthcare requires assembling provider roster, placing calls standardized script, recording wait times refusal rates, modelling disparities insurance type, race, geography. step involves bespoke data-engineering work research teams currently solve ad hoc: custom scripts loop around NPI API’s 1,200-record cap, manual regular expressions parse name fields, silent dplyr::left_join() calls multiply rows lookup table duplicates, hand-crafted Poisson models lack overdispersion diagnostics. mysterycall consolidates work single, tested, documented pipeline. provides taxonomy-based NPI search bypasses record cap, NANP phone validation state-geography checks, physician name parsing credential surname disambiguation, safe join wrappers enforce coverage uniqueness guarantees, drive-time isochrone generation, Census demographic overlay, Poisson mixed-effects modelling IRR reporting, publication-ready table map export. target users clinical researchers health-services researchers conduct mystery-caller audit studies need reproducible, auditable workflows rather one-scripts. mysterycall provides toolkit mystery caller audit studies evaluate patient access healthcare. handles full workflow: finding providers NPI registry, validating geocoding addresses, generating drive-time isochrones, overlaying Census demographics, producing publication-ready tables maps.

title: Mystery Caller Study Tools for Healthcare Access Research

title: Mystery Caller Study Tools for Healthcare Access Research
text: typical mystery caller study moves four stages:
code: library(mysterycall) library(dplyr)  # ── 1. Build a provider roster ────────────────────────────────────────────────  # Search by taxonomy across all 50 states (bypasses the 1,200-record API cap) all_states <- c(   "AL","AK","AZ","AR","CA","CO","CT","DE","FL","GA","HI","ID","IL","IN",   "IA","KS","KY","LA","ME","MD","MA","MI","MN","MS","MO","MT","NE","NV",   "NH","NJ","NM","NY","NC","ND","OH","OK","OR","PA","RI","SC","SD","TN",   "TX","UT","VT","VA","WA","WV","WI","WY" )  gyn_onc <- mysterycall_search_taxonomy("Gynecologic Oncology", states = all_states)  # Validate NPI numbers before downstream lookups gyn_onc_valid <- mysterycall_validate_npi(gyn_onc)  # Enrich with CMS Physician Compare demographics gyn_onc_enriched <- mysterycall_get_clinician_data(gyn_onc_valid)  # ── 2. Geocode ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  # Requires a Google Maps API key in GOOGLE_API_KEY env var geocoded <- mysterycall_geocode(   gyn_onc_enriched,   google_maps_api_key = Sys.getenv("GOOGLE_API_KEY") )  # ── 3. Drive-time isochrones ──────────────────────────────────────────────────  # Requires a routing API key in HERE_API_KEY env var isochrones <- mysterycall_isochrones_for_df(   geocoded,   breaks = c(1800, 3600, 7200, 10800)   # 30 / 60 / 120 / 180 min )  # Free the in-memory isochrone cache after a large batch mysterycall_clear_isochrone_cache()  # ── 4. Map ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  mysterycall_map_physicians(geocoded, popup_var = "name")

title: Internal: perform all cleaning steps common to both exported functions — .mc_clean_core
text: data data frame raw mystery-caller records (e.g. REDCap export).  Must data.frame subclass thereof. id_col Character scalar.  Column used identify unique physicians deduplication (first occurrence kept).  Set NULL skip deduplication. Default "phone". age_col Character scalar NULL.  Name numeric age column. NULL, age processing skipped entirely.  Default "age". age_breaks Numeric vector cut points passed base::cut(). Default c(-Inf, 50, 60, 70, Inf). age_labels Character vector category labels, length length(age_breaks) - 1. Default c("<50 yrs", "50-59 yrs", "60-69 yrs", ">=70 yrs"). wait_col Character scalar NULL.  Wait-time column (business days). Renamed "Business days appointment" output. Default "business_days_until_appointment". insurance_col Character scalar NULL. Default "insurance". Renamed "Insurance" output. gender_col Character scalar NULL. Default "gender". Renamed "Gender" output. credential_col Character scalar NULL. Column holding raw NPPES credential strings ("MD", "", etc.).  Default "Provider.Credential.Text". Renamed "Physician credential" output. academic_col Character scalar NULL. Default "academic_affiliation". Renamed "Academic affiliation" output. rurality_col Character scalar NULL. CBSA type column. Default "cbsatype10". Renamed "Rurality" output. central_col Character scalar NULL. Central-scheduling indicator column. Default "central_number_e_g_appointment_center". Renamed "Central scheduling" output. transfers_col Character scalar NULL. Number--transfers column.  recode applied; column kept -. Default NULL (skip). recode_credential Named character vector mapping raw credential values display labels. Default c("MD" = "Allopathic training", "" = "Osteopathic training"). recode_academic Named character vector mapping raw academic-affiliation values. Default c("University" = "Academic Practice"). recode_rurality Named character vector mapping raw CBSA-type values. Default c("Metro" = "Metropolitan area", "Micro" = "Rural area"). recode_central Named character vector mapping raw central-scheduling values. Default c("Yes" = "Yes, central scheduling"). drop_pii Logical.  TRUE (default), columns named first, last, middle, phone, address, notes, record_id, npi, zip (case-insensitive) removed output. fill_cols Character vector column names forward-fill (last-observation-carried-forward) recoding renaming. Uses tidyr::fill() package installed, zoo::na.locf(), pure-base-R loop. Columns absent data silently ignored. Default c("academic_affiliation", "cbsatype10"). keep_all Logical. TRUE, full column set (minus PII) returned.  FALSE, set standardized columns defined *_col parameters returned.

title: Distil key abstract numbers from fitted model objects — mysterycall_abstract_numbers
text: logistic_fit mysterycall_logistic_model object returned mysterycall_logistic_model(), NULL. Provides N, , CI, p-value primary binary outcome (appointment offered). poisson_fit mysterycall_poisson_model mysterycall_nb_model object, NULL. Provides N, IRR, CI, p-value wait time. lmm_fit mysterycall_lmm object returned mysterycall_lmm(), NULL. Provides N, beta coefficient, CI, p-value continuous wait time. LMM log-transformed ($log_transformed == TRUE), beta log-days scale unit label reflects . exposure_term Character scalar. exact term name extract model coefficient table (e.g. "insuranceMedicaid"). Must match term column or_table, irr_table, coef_table exactly. ref_label Character scalar. Human-readable reference group label used abstract sentence (e.g. "commercial insurance"). Default "reference group". comparison_label Character scalar NULL. Human-readable label comparison group (e.g. "Medicaid"). NULL (default), derived exposure_term stripping leading run lowercase letters (e.g. "insuranceMedicaid" becomes "Medicaid"). outcome_label Character scalar. Human-readable outcome description used abstract sentence. Default "appointment acceptance". digits_or Integer. Decimal places , IRR, beta coefficients. Default 2L. digits_p Integer. Decimal places p-values. Default 3L. acceptance_rate Named numeric vector length 2, NULL. form c(ref = 0.82, comparison = 0.61) provide raw acceptance rates reference comparison groups. Used compute absolute percentage-point gap. NULL (default), gap omitted sentence.

Odds ratio, NA_real_ logistic_fit NULL exposure_term found. or_ci character. Formatted "0.62 (0.41-0.94)", NA. or_p character. Formatted p-value (e.g. "0.024" "< 0.001"), NA. irr numeric. Incidence rate ratio, NA_real_. irr_ci character NA. irr_p character NA. beta numeric. LMM fixed-effect coefficient (days log-days), NA_real_. beta_ci character NA. beta_p character NA. absolute_gap numeric. ref_rate - comparison_rate proportion units, NA_real_ acceptance_rate NULL. abstract_sentence character. title: Distil key abstract numbers from fitted model objects — mysterycall_abstract_numbers
text: sentence assembled available components order: Lead: "Among [N] total calls, ". clause (logistic_fit non-NULL): primary clause. IRR clause (poisson_fit non-NULL): primary clause present; otherwise appended semicolon. LMM beta clause (lmm_fit non-NULL): primary clause IRR present; otherwise appended semicolon. Absolute gap suffix (acceptance_rate non-NULL): appended ", absolute [outcome_label] gap [X] percentage points ([ref]% vs. [comparison]%)".

title: Distil key abstract numbers from fitted model objects — mysterycall_abstract_numbers
code: # --- Minimal example: logistic fit only ------------------------------------- fake_logistic <- structure(   list(     n        = 412L,     or_table = data.frame(       term     = c("(Intercept)", "insuranceMedicaid"),       or       = c(2.10, 0.62),       ci_lower = c(1.20, 0.41),       ci_upper = c(3.68, 0.94),       p_value  = c(0.008, 0.024),       stringsAsFactors = FALSE     )   ),   class = "mysterycall_logistic_model" )  result <- mysterycall_abstract_numbers(   logistic_fit     = fake_logistic,   exposure_term    = "insuranceMedicaid",   ref_label        = "commercial insurance",   comparison_label = "Medicaid",   acceptance_rate  = c(ref = 0.82, comparison = 0.61) ) print(result) #> mysterycall_abstract_numbers #>  #>   n_total                   412 #>   OR                        0.62 #>   OR_CI                     0.41-0.94 #>   OR_full                   0.62 (0.41-0.94) #>   OR_p                      0.024 #>   absolute_gap_pct          21% #>   ref_rate_pct              82% #>   comparison_rate_pct       61% #>   abstract_sentence         #>     Among 412 total calls, Medicaid callers were 38% less likely to be #>     offered appointment acceptance than commercial insurance callers #>     (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.41-0.94, p=0.024), with an absolute appointment #>     acceptance gap of 21 percentage points (82% vs. 61%). #>  result$abstract_sentence #> [1] "Among 412 total calls, Medicaid callers were 38% less likely to be offered appointment acceptance than commercial insurance callers (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.41-0.94, p=0.024), with an absolute appointment acceptance gap of 21 percentage points (82% vs. 61%)."  # --- Extended example: logistic + Poisson fit ------------------------------- fake_poisson <- structure(   list(     n         = 298L,     irr_table = data.frame(       term      = c("(Intercept)", "insuranceMedicaid"),       irr       = c(0.95, 1.40),       ci_lower  = c(0.70, 1.12),       ci_upper  = c(1.29, 1.75),       p_value   = c(0.782, 0.003),       stringsAsFactors = FALSE     )   ),   class = "mysterycall_poisson_model" )  result2 <- mysterycall_abstract_numbers(   logistic_fit  = fake_logistic,   poisson_fit   = fake_poisson,   exposure_term = "insuranceMedicaid",   ref_label     = "commercial insurance",   acceptance_rate = c(ref = 0.82, comparison = 0.61) ) result2$abstract_sentence #> [1] "Among 412 total calls, Medicaid callers were 38% less likely to be offered appointment acceptance than commercial insurance callers (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.41-0.94, p=0.024); wait times were 40% longer (IRR 1.40, 95% CI 1.12-1.75, p=0.003), with an absolute appointment acceptance gap of 21 percentage points (82% vs. 61%)."

code: set.seed(42) n <- 80 df <- data.frame(   phone     = paste0("555-", formatC(seq_len(n), width = 4, flag = "0")),   insurance = rep(c("Medicaid", "Blue Cross/Blue Shield"), each = n / 2L),   reason_for_exclusions = sample(     c("Able to contact", "No answer", "Line disconnected"),     n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.75, 0.15, 0.10)   ),   business_days_until_appointment = ifelse(     stats::runif(n) > 0.3,     sample(1:30, n, replace = TRUE),     0L   ),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  ## Two-group comparison (Medicaid vs BCBS) res <- mysterycall_acceptance_rate_calc(   data             = df,   insurance_groups = c("Medicaid", "Blue Cross/Blue Shield") ) print(res) #> Medicaid acceptance rate: 20/26 = 76.9% (95% CI: 57.9%-89.0%) #> Blue Cross/Blue Shield acceptance rate: 23/31 = 74.2% (95% CI: 56.8%-86.3%)  #> Physicians accepted Medicaid at 76.9% vs Blue Cross/Blue Shield at 74.2%, a gap of 2.7 percentage points.  res$table #>                insurance n_total n_excluded n_numerator n_denominator rate_pct #> 1               Medicaid      40         14          20            26 76.92308 #> 2 Blue Cross/Blue Shield      40          9          23            31 74.19355 #>   ci_lower_pct ci_upper_pct #> 1     57.94845     88.96615 #> 2     56.75386     86.29829 #>                                                                      sentence #> 1               Medicaid acceptance rate: 20/26 = 76.9% (95% CI: 57.9%-89.0%) #> 2 Blue Cross/Blue Shield acceptance rate: 23/31 = 74.2% (95% CI: 56.8%-86.3%)  ## Without wait-time filter res2 <- mysterycall_acceptance_rate_calc(   data      = df,   wait_col  = NULL ) res2$sentences #> [1] "Blue Cross/Blue Shield acceptance rate: 31/31 = 100.0% (95% CI: 89.0%-100.0%)" #> [2] "Medicaid acceptance rate: 26/26 = 100.0% (95% CI: 87.1%-100.0%)"

what: Automatically select and compare wait-time models — mysterycall_auto_model
title: Automatically select and compare wait-time models — mysterycall_auto_model
text: Fits Poisson GLMM first, checks overdispersion, upgrades negative binomial GLMM warranted. Optionally fits Linear Mixed Model (LMM) parallel evaluates whether defensible communication/sensitivity tool. Returns statistically preferred count model structured recommendation attached.

title: Automatically select and compare wait-time models — mysterycall_auto_model

title: Automatically select and compare wait-time models — mysterycall_auto_model
text: data data frame. outcome Character scalar. Name count (wait-day) outcome column. predictors Character vector fixed-effect column names. random_intercept Character scalar. Grouping column physician random intercept. phi_threshold Numeric. Pearson phi NB model replaces Poisson. Default 2.0. conf_level Numeric. Confidence level Wald CIs. Default 0.95. include_lmm Logical. Fit LMM evaluate suitability? Default TRUE. LMM never primary model; always secondary communication/sensitivity check. lmm_normality_threshold Numeric. Shapiro-Wilk p-value threshold LMM residuals considered approximately normal. Default 0.05. ... Additional arguments forwarded model-fitting functions.

title: Automatically select and compare wait-time models — mysterycall_auto_model
text: selected count model - either mysterycall_poisson_model mysterycall_nb_model - extra element $selection: poisson_phi Numeric. Overdispersion initial Poisson fit. model_chosen Character. "poisson" "negative_binomial". reason Character. Explanation count-model selection. lmm mysterycall_lmm object, NULL include_lmm = FALSE fitting failed. lmm_shapiro_p Numeric. Shapiro-Wilk p-value LMM residuals, NA. lmm_defensible Logical. TRUE LMM residuals pass normality outcome range exceeds 30 days. lmm_recommendation Character. Plain-language guidance whether use LMM. recommendation Character. Overall one-paragraph guidance covering primary model LMM.

title: Automatically select and compare wait-time models — mysterycall_auto_model
text: Decision tree Fit Poisson GLMM compute Pearson overdispersion (phi). phi <= phi_threshold: primary model = Poisson. Otherwise: re-fit negative binomial (NB) GLMM. include_lmm = TRUE: fit LMM run Shapiro-Wilk normality test residuals. residuals approximately normal (p >= lmm_normality_threshold) outcome range exceeds 30 days, LMM flagged defensible reporting day-scale coefficients alongside primary count model. Otherwise LMM flagged recommended. primary return value selected count model (Poisson NB) class mysterycall_poisson_model() / mysterycall_nb_model(), downstream functions work unchanged. LMM routing metadata live result$selection.

title: Automatically select and compare wait-time models — mysterycall_auto_model
code: set.seed(1978) df <- data.frame(   wait = rpois(60, 18),   ins  = rep(c("Medicaid", "BCBS"), 30),   phys = rep(paste0("Dr_", 1:10), each = 6),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) result <- mysterycall_auto_model(df, "wait", "ins", "phys") #> Step 1/3: Fitting Poisson GLMM to assess overdispersion... #> Fitting Poisson GLMER: wait ~ ins + (1 | phys) #> boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular') #> Convergence issues detected: #>   boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular') #> Consider simplifying predictors or using nAGQ = 1. #> Singular fit: random-intercept variance is ~0. The physician-level random effect explains little variation. #> Model fitted: n=60, physicians=10, AIC=340.4, overdispersion=0.86 #> Poisson GLMM selected: phi = 0.86 <= 2.0 (no overdispersion detected).  #> Step 3/3: Fitting LMM to evaluate day-scale coefficients... #> Fitting LMM: wait ~ ins + (1 | phys) #> boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular') #> Model fitted: n=60, physicians=10, AIC=342.6, sigma=3.93, R2m=0.095, R2c=0.095 print(result) #> Poisson GLMER  n = 60  physicians = 10  AIC = 340.4  BIC = 346.7 #>   Warning: convergence warnings; singular fit #>   Reference levels: ins='BCBS' #>  #> Fixed effects (IRR with Wald CI): #>          term    irr ci_lower ci_upper p_value_fmt #> 1 (Intercept) 17.000   15.587   18.541      <0.001 #> 2 insMedicaid  1.149    1.020    1.294       0.022 #>  #> Random intercept (phys):  variance = 0.0000  SD = 0.0000 #>  #> === Auto-Model Selection === #> Count model: poisson (Poisson phi = 0.86) #> LMM: Shapiro-Wilk p = 0.830  |  Defensible: NO #>  #> --- Recommendation --- #> PRIMARY MODEL: Poisson GLMM (phi = 0.86 <= 2.0; no overdispersion). Report #>   incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with 95% Wald CIs. SENSITIVITY / #>   COMMUNICATION: LMM is not recommended: outcome range = 17 days (< 30). A #>   floor effect near zero violates the normality assumption. Stick with the #>   Poisson GLMM. Do not report LMM coefficients as primary results. #>

LMM assumes approximate normality; with a narrow range the distribution may be non-normal or floor-censored. Consider Poisson/NB GLMM instead and check the Q-Q plot. #> Warning: Convergence issues detected: #>   boundary (singular) fit: see help('isSingular') #> Warning: Singular fit: physician random-intercept variance is ~0. Consider a fixed-effects-only model. print(res) #> Calendar vs. Business Days Sensitivity Analysis #>   Calendar model: n = 60  |  Business model: n = 60 #>   Direction consistent across all terms: NO -- see Consistent column #>  #>              Term               Calendar days              Business days #>    scenarioSingle  0 (-5.8 to 5.8), p = 1.000 2 (-1.4 to 5.3), p = 0.265 #>  scenarioStraight -1 (-6.8 to 4.8), p = 0.736 2 (-1.4 to 5.4), p = 0.253 #>  Consistent #>         Yes #>          No #>  #> -- Supplemental paragraph -- #> As a pre-specified sensitivity analysis, we repeated the secondary wait-time #> analysis substituting business days (Monday through Friday, excluding the 11 #> U.S. federal holidays) for calendar days. Business days were computed using the #> R package \emph{bizdays} with a US Federal holiday calendar. The calendar-day #> model included 60 observations with a recorded appointment date; the #> business-day model included 60 observations. Both models used the same #> mixed-effects linear regression specification (scenario as fixed effect #> compared with Straight couple (reference); physician practice as random #> intercept). Results were directionally consistent for most comparisons, with #> the exception of scenarioStraight. Shapiro-Wilk normality tests on model #> residuals: calendar-day model: W = 0.971, p = 0.168; business-day model: W = #> 0.981, p = 0.464. Full results are presented in Supplemental Table S2.

title: Detect and visualise calendar and sequence drift in mystery-caller outcomes — mysterycall_caller_drift
text: Calendar drift. outcome_col aggregated week_or_day period. linear model lm(rate \~ time_index) fitted, time_index chronological rank period (1, 2, 3, ...). slope estimated change acceptance rate per week (day). Week boundaries follow format(date, "%Y-%U") (Sunday-start ISO-adjacent convention). Sequence drift. Calls grouped consecutive bins five call_seq_col (within-caller date rank call_seq_col NULL). Within bin acceptance rate mean sequence number computed. linear model lm(rate \~ mean_seq) fitted; slope estimated change acceptance rate per additional call. Significance assessed \(\alpha = 0.05\).

title: Detect and visualise calendar and sequence drift in mystery-caller outcomes — mysterycall_caller_drift
code: set.seed(42) n <- 120L df <- data.frame(   call_date = seq(as.Date("2023-01-02"), by = "day", length.out = n),   caller    = rep(c("Alice", "Bob", "Carol"), times = n / 3L),   offered   = rbinom(n, 1L, 0.55) )  # Calendar + sequence drift (sequence derived from date within caller) res <- mysterycall_caller_drift(   df,   outcome_col = "offered",   date_col    = "call_date",   caller_col  = "caller",   week_or_day = "week",   plot        = FALSE ) cat(res$sentence, "\n") #> Acceptance rates did not change significantly over the study period (slope=+0.001 per week, p=0.91) or over call sequence (slope=+0.002 per call, p=0.41), supporting design validity.  res$calendar$p_value #> [1] 0.905223 head(res$calendar$rate_by_period) #>    period time_index      rate n #> 1 2023-01          1 0.3333333 6 #> 2 2023-02          2 0.2857143 7 #> 3 2023-03          3 0.5714286 7 #> 4 2023-04          4 0.5714286 7 #> 5 2023-05          5 0.2857143 7 #> 6 2023-06          6 0.5714286 7  # Explicit call_seq_col, no plot df$seq <- ave(seq_len(n), df$caller, FUN = seq_along) res2 <- mysterycall_caller_drift(   df,   outcome_col  = "offered",   call_seq_col = "seq",   plot         = FALSE ) res2$sequence$slope #> [1] 0.002222222

title: Clean raw mystery-caller data for publication-ready analysis — mysterycall_clean_data
text: data data frame raw mystery-caller records (e.g. REDCap export).  Must data.frame subclass thereof. id_col Character scalar.  Column used identify unique physicians deduplication (first occurrence kept).  Set NULL skip deduplication. Default "phone". age_col Character scalar NULL.  Name numeric age column. NULL, age processing skipped entirely.  Default "age". age_breaks Numeric vector cut points passed base::cut(). Default c(-Inf, 50, 60, 70, Inf). age_labels Character vector category labels, length length(age_breaks) - 1. Default c("<50 yrs", "50-59 yrs", "60-69 yrs", ">=70 yrs"). wait_col Character scalar NULL.  Wait-time column (business days). Renamed "Business days appointment" output. Default "business_days_until_appointment". insurance_col Character scalar NULL. Default "insurance". Renamed "Insurance" output. gender_col Character scalar NULL. Default "gender". Renamed "Gender" output. credential_col Character scalar NULL. Column holding raw NPPES credential strings ("MD", "", etc.).  Default "Provider.Credential.Text". Renamed "Physician credential" output. academic_col Character scalar NULL. Default "academic_affiliation". Renamed "Academic affiliation" output. rurality_col Character scalar NULL. CBSA type column. Default "cbsatype10". Renamed "Rurality" output. central_col Character scalar NULL. Central-scheduling indicator column. Default "central_number_e_g_appointment_center". Renamed "Central scheduling" output. transfers_col Character scalar NULL. Number--transfers column.  recode applied; column kept -. Default NULL (skip). recode_credential Named character vector mapping raw credential values display labels. Default c("MD" = "Allopathic training", "" = "Osteopathic training"). recode_academic Named character vector mapping raw academic-affiliation values. Default c("University" = "Academic Practice"). recode_rurality Named character vector mapping raw CBSA-type values. Default c("Metro" = "Metropolitan area", "Micro" = "Rural area"). recode_central Named character vector mapping raw central-scheduling values. Default c("Yes" = "Yes, central scheduling"). drop_pii Logical.  TRUE (default), columns named first, last, middle, phone, address, notes, record_id, npi, zip (case-insensitive) removed output. fill_cols Character vector column names forward-fill (last-observation-carried-forward) recoding renaming. title: Compute Disparity Metrics Across Groups — mysterycall_disparities_table

title: Compute Disparity Metrics Across Groups — mysterycall_disparities_table
